$comment: How large a request body each host will buffer before refusing it, and what
it answers when the body is larger.
Three endpoints, four implementations, and until this file existed the only
thing holding them together was a comment in one of them saying it used the
'same bound as the native host':
- crates/ruvyxa_dev_server                       (`dev`, `start`, `preview`)
- crates/ruvyxa_cli/src/build.rs                 writes the effective policy
into build.json for a deploy
- packages/ruvyxa/runtime/serverless-handler.mjs every deployed build
- packages/@ruvyxa/core/src/standalone-server.ts the six self-hosted adapters
The build.rs row is the one that makes a split invisible. A deployed build
does not read the native host's constants; it reads the numbers `ruvyxa
build` wrote into the manifest, and those were four bare literals beside
the config lookups -- `unwrap_or(1024 * 1024)` and its three neighbours.
Change a default on the native host and every deployed build keeps the old
one, for exactly the projects that configured nothing and so have no value
in the manifest to correct it. That is the shape `defaultMaxWidth` shipped
in: one Rust constant against unnamed copies written into deployed
functions, which no name-matching gate can see. build.rs names the
constants now, and this table holds the two languages.
Every implementation replays this file:
- crates/ruvyxa_dev_server/src/lib.rs                     (native host and
the manifest writer)
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/serverless-shared-tables.test.mjs (the deployed
handler and the
standalone server
it generates)
$axumNote: On the native host a number in a handler is not the bound until a layer
says so. Axum applies `DefaultBodyLimit` -- 2 MiB unless a route overrides
it -- while extracting `Bytes`, which happens before the handler runs, so
`POST /__ruvyxa/rsc` refused a 3 MiB server-function call that every
deployed build accepted, and `serverFunction.bytes` below described
nothing. Its two neighbours had carried a layer from the start, which is
what made the third look deliberate.
chain in the direction the guard reads: from the handlers that extract a
body to the routes that register them.
$statusNote: 413 is the whole of the refusal contract. The message text deliberately is
not: the native host's API branch appends the read error to it, because a
body that was cut short and a body that was too large arrive at the same
place and an operator needs to tell them apart.
`message` is a claim about the source, not about the wire, and only the
deployed hosts put it on the wire at all. On the native host a body over
the limit is refused by the `DefaultBodyLimit` layer during extraction,
which answers with axum's own text -- so `/__ruvyxa/action` and
`POST /__ruvyxa/rsc` never reach the string beside them. That is the cost
of bounding the allocation before the handler runs, and it is the same
arrangement both routes have. It is recorded here so that a rename of
either string is a decision rather than an accident, and so that nobody
writes a test asserting the native host emits one.
$ceilingNote: `configCeiling` is enforced by the Rust config validator alone, which is
correct rather than a gap: a deployed build reads a manifest `ruvyxa build`
already validated, and re-checking a number the same toolchain wrote would
be a second opinion about a decision already made. It is here so that
raising a default past its own ceiling fails a test instead of a project's
